transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hi Siân, come in. And who's this?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is my partner, Tom. He's just here for support.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Hi.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hi, Tom. Siân, is it all right for Tom to be here while we talk?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, that's fine.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What's been happening?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I keep having these panic attacks. Out of nowhere. My heart races, I can't breathe, my hands tingle, and I honestly think I'm going to die.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: That sounds really frightening. How long have they been happening?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: About four months. Since around the start of summer.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How often?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Two or three times a week now. It's getting worse.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How long does each one last?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Ten minutes or so, but I feel wiped out after.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Have you changed what you do because of them?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I avoid supermarkets now. And I won't get on the Underground. Tom does all the shopping.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I don't mind. But she used to love going into town.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: In between attacks, do you worry about having another one?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: All the time. And I worry about everything else too. Work, money, everything.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How's your sleep?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It's okay, actually. I get off to sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And your mood? Have you been feeling down or hopeless?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A bit fed up, but not depressed, I don't think.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I have to ask everyone this. Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No. Never.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thank you. How much caffeine do you have? Coffee, tea, energy drinks?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: About four coffees a day. Well, six if I count the ones at work.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Six, then. Any alcohol?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A couple of glasses of wine at the weekend.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any drugs?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How are things at work?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm managing. I work in marketing. I haven't had any time off.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I'm actually off at the moment with stress myself. Work's been awful. It's not been an easy few months for either of us.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'm sorry to hear that, Tom. It might be worth you speaking to your own GP too.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Yeah, I've got an appointment.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Siân, have you had any problems with your heart or thyroid?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No. You checked my thyroid last month and it was normal.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Yes, I've got that here, it was normal. Any medicines? Any allergies?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, nothing. No allergies.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Your questionnaire scores today: GAD-7 is 15 and PHQ-9 is 8. That fits with significant anxiety, with panic disorder, rather than depression.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay. So what can I do?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: The treatment with the best evidence for panic disorder is a talking therapy called CBT. I'll give you the details to refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: We could also try a medicine, an SSRI called sertraline, alongside the therapy. Would you like to?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I think so. I need something.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: We start low because it can make anxiety a bit worse for the first week or two. Take 25 milligrams once a day for a week, then go up to 50 milligrams once a day.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'd like to see you in two weeks to see how you're getting on with it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: It would also help to cut down the coffee gradually.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That'll be hard.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Gradually is fine. And if you ever do have thoughts of harming yourself, call 111 and choose the mental health option, or the Samaritans on 116 123.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thank you.

reference_note.history: Recurrent panic attacks with palpitations, breathlessness, hand tingling and fear of dying, lasting about 10 minutes, now two to three times weekly and increasing. Anticipatory anxiety and generalised worry. Avoids supermarkets and the Underground. Sleep satisfactory. Mood 'fed up' but not depressed. No thoughts of self-harm or suicide. Caffeine: about six coffees a day (initially said four). Alcohol: a couple of glasses of wine at weekends. No drug use. Works in marketing; no time off. Partner is off work with stress and has his own GP appointment. Thyroid function normal last month.
reference_note.medications_allergies: No regular medications. No known drug allergies.
reference_note.impression: Panic disorder with agoraphobic avoidance and generalised anxiety symptoms. No risk to self identified.
reference_note.plan: Self-referral details for NHS Talking Therapies (CBT). Start sertraline 25 mg once daily for 1 week, then 50 mg once daily; warned of possible initial increase in anxiety. Review in 2 weeks after starting sertraline. Reduce caffeine gradually.
reference_note.safety_netting: If thoughts of self-harm, call NHS 111 (mental health option) or Samaritans 116 123.
